simple: This page is about `VectorForce`, a constraint that keeps pushing a part with the same amount of force all the time. You choose the push's direction and strength with a `Vector3`. Because the push never stops, the part keeps speeding up unless something slows it down. It is perfect for rockets, jet packs, or wind.
analogy: It is like a rocket engine that is always on full blast: it does not care how fast you are already going, it just keeps pushing.
keyPoints: `VectorForce` applies a constant force to an assembly, so the part keeps accelerating.
The `Force` property is a `Vector3` that sets both direction and strength.
Since it never stops pushing, parts can reach very high speeds. Use `LinearVelocity` if you want a steady speed instead.
For just a starting push, set `AssemblyLinearVelocity` once instead.
Force is applied at `Attachment0`'s spot by default, which can also make the part spin. Turn on `ApplyAtCenterOfMass` to push from the middle.
`RelativeTo = Attachment0` (default): the push turns with the part, like a rocket thruster always pushing the rocket forward.
`RelativeTo = World`: the push always goes the same world direction, like wind.
`RelativeTo = Attachment1`: the push follows the rotation of the other attachment.

terms.constraint: An object that controls how parts move, like an invisible motor, rope, or hand pushing them. Mover constraints push or spin parts for you.
terms.assembly: A group of parts that are welded or joined together so physics moves them as one piece. A car body plus its welded seats is one assembly.
terms.attachment: A small invisible point you put inside a part. Constraints hook onto attachments, the same way a rope ties onto a hook.
terms.Attachment0 / Attachment1: The two attachment slots a constraint uses. Attachment0 is usually the one that gets pushed; Attachment1 is the other end or the reference point.
terms.force: A push or pull. More force on the same part means it speeds up faster.
terms.constant force: A push that stays the same size the whole time.
terms.acceleration: How quickly speed changes. Constant force means the speed keeps going up and up.
terms.center of mass: The balance point of an object. Pushing anywhere else can make it spin as well as move.
terms.world coordinates: Directions based on the world's fixed X, Y, and Z axes. (0, 100, 0) always means straight up.
terms.relative to Attachment0: Directions are measured from the attachment's own facing. (0, 100, 0) means 'up' from the attachment's point of view, which changes if the part tips over.
terms.gravity: The pull downward on every unanchored part. To float a part, the upward force must equal its mass times `workspace.Gravity`.

example.title: Make a part float by cancelling gravity
example.place: Script inside a Part in Workspace (part not Anchored)
example.code:
local part = script.Parent

local attachment = Instance.new("Attachment")
attachment.Parent = part

local force = Instance.new("VectorForce")
force.Attachment0 = attachment
force.RelativeTo = Enum.ActuatorRelativeTo.World
force.ApplyAtCenterOfMass = true

-- Push up exactly as hard as gravity pulls down
local mass = part.AssemblyMass
force.Force = Vector3.new(0, mass * workspace.Gravity, 0)
force.Parent = part
explain: We add an attachment and create a `VectorForce` linked to it.
`RelativeTo = World` so 'up' always means world up, even if the part tilts.
`ApplyAtCenterOfMass = true` so the push does not make the part spin.
Gravity pulls with a force of mass times `workspace.Gravity`, so we push up with exactly that much.
The forces cancel out, so the part floats. Add a little more force and it slowly rises faster and faster.

watchOut: A push even a little bigger than gravity makes the part speed up forever and fly away. Use `LinearVelocity` for steady speed.
If the part spins unexpectedly, the force is off-center. Turn on `ApplyAtCenterOfMass`.
With the default `RelativeTo = Attachment0`, if the part flips over, 'up' becomes 'down'. Use `World` for wind-like pushes.
